designGate.prompt: Before writing code, sketch what a scope actually stores about a name it knows -- not just 'a dict', but what the different things it can say about that name are. Then say what a scope's next link is when a name isn't found locally: is that always 'ask my parent', or can the answer depend on something that isn't fixed when the scope is created? Name both.
requiredElements: per-scope binding table named (what a scope stores about a name it owns)
how a scope's next link is determined when a name isn't declared locally

parts.title: Nested lexical scopes

hints.text: What do you need to answer lookup(name) quickly: one flat table for everything, or something that remembers where each scope came from?
Give each scope its own dict of name -> type, plus a fixed reference to whichever scope was current when it was created. lookup checks its own dict first, then follows that reference outward.

A Scope holds {id, parent, bindings: dict[name, type]}. Keep scopes[None] = root from the start, and a stack of currently-open scopes (starts as [root]) so enter_scope pushes, exit_scope pops (raising if the stack is down to just root), and declare/lookup always act on the top of the stack.

probes: A scope chain as a linked stack of open scopes, versus a flat map from scope_id to parent -- which did you pick?
Why is there no way, in this part, to touch a scope you're not currently standing in -- what's the simplest thing that would have to change to allow it?

parts.title: Read and declare into any scope by id

hints.text: lookup and declare now take an optional scope argument. What has to change so a name that isn't found locally can point somewhere that isn't a parent at all?
Give each scope a small table where each name maps to one of two things: its own declaration, or a pointer to another scope that has it. A plain parent-walk only ever finds the first kind.

bindings[name] holds either ('own', typ) or ('redirect', target_scope). declare(name, typ, scope) writes ('own', typ) onto scope's own table and ('redirect', scope) onto the current scope's table -- check both preconditions before writing either, so a raise leaves nothing half-done. lookup walks: own returns it, redirect jumps straight to the target's own table (which always has it, by construction), missing goes up to parent. Resolve the scope argument against a dict of every scope ever created, keyed by id -- passed explicitly (including None, which is root's own id), it targets that scope; left out, it means the top of the stack.

probes: What did part 2 cost the structure you picked in part 1 -- the plain single walk up parents doesn't work anymore, so what changed?
A redirect is a third thing a scope can say about a name, next to 'mine' and 'not mine.' Where did you put it, and does lookup still have one code path?

parts.title: Dynamic scopes

hints.text: Two scopes can now share an id and a set of declarations, but disagree at different times about what's above them. What single fact -- not something you can store on the scope forever -- decides which?
A dynamic scope's next link isn't a fixed field. It's whoever is directly below it on the current stack of open scopes, right now. A lexical scope's parent is still fixed, exactly as before.

Give each scope a dynamic: bool, set only at creation and never touched again. The next-link function checks: at root, stop. If dynamic, the scope must currently be on the open stack -- raise if not, otherwise its next link is whoever is directly below it there. Otherwise (lexical), its next link is the fixed parent. Before walking a lookup's chain for a name, walk this same next-link function from the target all the way to root once, up front -- that single pass is what makes even a dynamic scope's own declarations unreachable while it's closed, not just the ones further up.

probes: Part 2 fixed a scope's parent at creation. Now some scopes have no fixed parent at all -- is 'parent' still one field in your model?
Is 'is this scope askable' a property of the scope itself, or of the whole path above it?

criteria: the two-caller dynamic-entry example and the lexical-under-closed-dynamic-ancestor example both resolve exactly as specified
a single per-scope binding table expresses 'mine', 'redirect to elsewhere', and 'not mine' without a name collision between the first two
dynamic resolution reads the live stack of open scopes rather than a field stored permanently on the scope
one next-link / resolution code path shared by every part, not a special case bolted on per feature
no separate 'is this scope askable' pass duplicated from the resolution walk itself
declared-elsewhere and dynamic-entry edge cases considered before being told
stated why a closed dynamic scope's own declarations are unreachable, not just the ones further up its chain
